cemc-galois-2015-01a.title: Walk down the line
cemc-galois-2015-01a.body:
The $y$-intercept of line 1 is $6$ and the slope is $2$: each step of 1 to the left lowers $y$ by 2. To lower $y$ from 6 to 0 we go $3$ units left, to $x = -3$.

**Answer: $-3$**

cemc-galois-2015-01b.title: Slope–intercept form
cemc-galois-2015-01b.body:
Line 2 is $y = -3x + b$. Since $Q(3,12)$ is on it, $12 = -9 + b$, so $b = 21$.

**Answer: $y = -3x + 21$**

cemc-galois-2015-01c.title: Base on the x-axis
cemc-galois-2015-01c.body:
Line 2 is $y = -3x + 21$ (part (b)); setting $y = 0$ gives $x = 7$, so $R = (7, 0)$. Also $P = (-3, 0)$.

Base $PR = 7 - (-3) = 10$; the height is the $y$-coordinate of $Q$, which is $12$. Area $= \frac12 \cdot 10 \cdot 12 = 60$.

**Answer: 60**

cemc-galois-2015-02b.title: Use the percentage gap
cemc-galois-2015-02b.body:
The gap is $50\% - 30\% = 20\%$ of the 240 students: $0.2 \times 240 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

cemc-galois-2015-02c.title: Count riders
cemc-galois-2015-02c.body:
School C: $0.45 \times 200 = 90$ riders. Combined: $0.576 \times 500 = 288$ riders. So School D had $288 - 90 = 198$ riders out of 300, which is $\frac{198}{300} = 66\%$.

**Answer: $x = 66$**

cemc-galois-2015-02d.title: Set up an inequality
cemc-galois-2015-02d.body:
School E has $\frac{n}{100} \cdot 200 = 2n$ riders and School F has $\frac{2n}{100} \cdot 250 = 5n$ riders, so $7n$ of the 450 students got a ride.

We need $0.55 \cdot 450 < 7n < 0.60 \cdot 450$, i.e. $247.5 < 7n < 270$, so $35.36\ldots < n < 38.57\ldots$

The positive integers in this range are $n = 36, 37, 38$. (Check: $7 \cdot 36 = 252$ and $7 \cdot 38 = 266$ both lie between 247.5 and 270.)

**Answer: $n = 36, 37, 38$**

cemc-galois-2015-02d.title: Combined percentage directly
cemc-galois-2015-02d.body:
The combined percentage is $\dfrac{7n}{450} \cdot 100\% = \dfrac{14n}{9}\%$. We need $55 < \frac{14n}{9} < 60$, i.e. $495 < 14n < 540$. Since $14 \cdot 35 = 490$, $14 \cdot 36 = 504$, $14 \cdot 38 = 532$, $14 \cdot 39 = 546$, the values are $n = 36, 37, 38$.

**Answer: $n = 36, 37, 38$**

cemc-galois-2015-03a.title: Parity rules
cemc-galois-2015-03a.body:
$5$ is odd. An odd number plus an even number is odd, so $n$ cannot be even. An odd plus an odd is even, so $n$ is odd.

**Answer: odd**

cemc-galois-2015-03a.title: Subtract
cemc-galois-2015-03a.body:
$n = (n + 5) - 5$ is an even number minus an odd number, which is odd. (Example: $n + 5 = 8$ gives $n = 3$.)

**Answer: odd**

cemc-galois-2015-03b.title: Case on parity
cemc-galois-2015-03b.body:
A product of integers is even as soon as one factor is even.

- If $c$ or $d$ is even, then the factor $c$ or $d$ makes $cd(c+d)$ even.
- Otherwise $c$ and $d$ are both odd, so $c + d$ (odd + odd) is even, and again $cd(c+d)$ is even.

So $cd(c+d)$ is always even. ∎

cemc-galois-2015-03b.title: Work modulo 2
cemc-galois-2015-03b.body: Modulo 2 each of $c, d$ is $0$ or $1$. If $c \equiv 0$ or $d \equiv 0$ the product is $\equiv 0$. If $c \equiv d \equiv 1$ then $c + d \equiv 0$. In every case $cd(c+d) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$. ∎

cemc-galois-2015-03c.title: Use prime factorization
cemc-galois-2015-03c.body:
$300 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^2$. For $e + f$ to be odd, one of $e, f$ must be odd, so the other contains all of $2^2$. The odd one is an odd divisor $d$ of 300, i.e. a divisor of $75 = 3 \cdot 5^2$, which has $2 \cdot 3 = 6$ divisors. Each $d$ gives the pair $\{d, 300/d\}$ (the two numbers are never equal, and different $d$ give different pairs), and ordering it so that $e < f$ gives exactly one ordered pair. So there are 6.

**Answer: 6**

cemc-galois-2015-03d.title: Factor pairs of opposite parity
cemc-galois-2015-03d.body:
Let $a = m + 1$ and $b = 2n + m$. Then $b - a = 2n - 1$ is odd and positive, so $a < b$ and $a, b$ have opposite parity. Conversely, any factorization $9000 = ab$ with $1 < a < b$ and $a, b$ of opposite parity gives $m = a - 1 \ge 1$ and $n = \frac{b - a + 1}{2} \ge 1$, an integer. So we count such factorizations.

$9000 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5^3$. Opposite parity means one factor gets all of $2^3$ and the other is odd. Write the odd parts as $r s = 1125 = 3^2 \cdot 5^3$, which has $3 \cdot 4 = 12$ divisors. Each divisor $r$ of 1125 gives the factorization $\{8r, 1125/r\}$; these 12 unordered pairs are distinct and none has equal parts. The only one with smaller part equal to 1 is $\{1, 9000\}$ (which would give $m = 0$). So there are $12 - 1 = 11$ pairs.

**Answer: 11**

cemc-galois-2015-04a.title: Supplementary angles
cemc-galois-2015-04a.body:
$E, X, D$ lie on a line, so $\angle YXE + \angle YXD = 180^\circ$. Since $Z = D$, $\angle YXD = \angle YXZ = 60^\circ$ (equilateral triangle). So $\angle YXE = 120^\circ$.

**Answer: $120^\circ$**

cemc-galois-2015-04a.title: Exterior angle
cemc-galois-2015-04a.body:
$\angle YXE$ is an exterior angle of the equilateral triangle at $X$, so it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, $60^\circ + 60^\circ = 120^\circ$.

**Answer: $120^\circ$**

cemc-galois-2015-04b.title: Track the square move by move
cemc-galois-2015-04b.body:
Each rotation stops when a side of the square meets a side of the triangle. When a side of the triangle lies along a side of the square and we rotate about the triangle vertex in the *middle* of the square's side, the rotation is $180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$; when we rotate about a triangle vertex sitting at a *corner* of the square, it is $90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$. Tracking the position:

| After move | Square vertex at a triangle vertex | Triangle side on square side |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | $D = Z$ | $XZ$ on $DE$ |
| 1 (about $X$, $120^\circ$) | $E = Y$ | $XY$ on $DE$ |
| 2 (about $Y$, $30^\circ$) | $E = Y$ | $YZ$ on $EB$ |
| 3 (about $Z$, $120^\circ$) | $B = X$ | $ZX$ on $EB$ |
| 4 (about $X$, $30^\circ$) | $B = X$ | $XY$ on $BC$ |
| 5 (about $Y$, $120^\circ$) | $C = Z$ | $YZ$ on $BC$ |
| 6 (about $Z$, $30^\circ$) | $C = Z$ | $ZX$ on $CD$ |
| 7 (about $X$, $120^\circ$) | $D = Y$ | $XY$ on $CD$ |

After moves 1–6 the corners of the square at triangle vertices are $E, E, B, B, C, C$; after move 7 it is $D$ (at $Y$). So $D$ next coincides with a vertex of the triangle after **7** moves.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-galois-2015-04c.title: Arcs over one full cycle
cemc-galois-2015-04c.body:
Continue the table of part (b): move 8 is about $Y$ through $30^\circ$, after which $D = Y$ and $YZ$ lies along $DE$ — the same *relative* position as at the start, but with the triangle's labels shifted ($D$ at $Y$ instead of $Z$). The next move is again a $120^\circ$ rotation, now about $Z$. So every 8 moves the pattern repeats with labels cycled $Z \to Y \to X \to Z$, and the square first returns to its original position after $3 \times 8 = 24$ moves. By symmetry, $E$ travels the same distance in each block of 8 moves.

In each move $E$ travels an arc of a circle centred at the pivot, with radius = distance from $E$ to the pivot (side 2, so midpoints of sides are at distance 1 from the adjacent corners, $\sqrt{2^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt5$ from the far corners of the square, and $EC = 2\sqrt2$):

| Move | Pivot position on square | Radius from $E$ | Angle |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $X$ at midpoint of $ED$ | 1 | $120^\circ$ |
| 2 | $Y$ at $E$ | 0 | $30^\circ$ |
| 3 | $Z$ at midpoint of $EB$ | 1 | $120^\circ$ |
| 4 | $X$ at $B$ | 2 | $30^\circ$ |
| 5 | $Y$ at midpoint of $BC$ | $\sqrt5$ | $120^\circ$ |
| 6 | $Z$ at $C$ | $2\sqrt2$ | $30^\circ$ |
| 7 | $X$ at midpoint of $CD$ | $\sqrt5$ | $120^\circ$ |
| 8 | $Y$ at $D$ | 2 | $30^\circ$ |

An arc of angle $\theta$ and radius $\rho$ has length $\frac{\theta}{360^\circ} \cdot 2\pi\rho$; $120^\circ$ gives $\frac{2\pi}{3}\rho$ and $30^\circ$ gives $\frac{\pi}{6}\rho$. Total over 8 moves:
$$\tfrac{2\pi}{3}(1 + 1 + \sqrt5 + \sqrt5) + \tfrac{\pi}{6}(0 + 2 + 2\sqrt2 + 2) = \tfrac{4\pi}{3} + \tfrac{4\sqrt5\pi}{3} + \tfrac{2\pi}{3} + \tfrac{\sqrt2\pi}{3} = 2\pi + \tfrac{4\sqrt5}{3}\pi + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\pi.$$
Over 24 moves: $3$ times this, $6\pi + 4\sqrt5\,\pi + \sqrt2\,\pi$.

**Answer: $6\pi + 4\sqrt5\,\pi + \sqrt2\,\pi$**
